learningObjective: Explain why the Triton paper introduces a tile-level IR, positioned between CUDA-thread and pure tensor abstractions.

canonicalClaims.claim: The Triton paper introduces a tile-level (block-of-elements) programming abstraction so that per-thread bookkeeping (indices, coalescing, shared-memory staging, register tiling) is handled by the compiler while the user still controls block sizes, memory access patterns via block pointers/offsets, and program-level parallelism, striking a middle ground between raw CUDA (thread-level) and high-level tensor libraries.
conditions: The programmer writes kernels at the tile granularity (a program processes a block of elements).
The compiler is responsible for translating tile-level ops into per-thread PTX with vectorization, coalescing and shared-memory usage.
nonImplications: Does not imply Triton is faster than hand-tuned CUDA on every kernel; it targets productivity + competitive performance for many common ops.
Does not imply the tile-level IR eliminates the need to think about memory access patterns; users still choose block shapes and offsets.

misconceptions.claim: Triton exposes the same thread/warp/block hierarchy as CUDA; programmers still write per-thread indexing manually.
misconceptions.whyWrong: The paper's key departure from CUDA is to hide per-thread indexing behind tile-level ops; the compiler emits per-thread code from tile-level programs.

misconceptions.claim: Triton is a Python DSL that compiles to NumPy; it does not target GPU hardware.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Triton compiles Python-embedded tile-level kernels to GPU PTX (via LLVM), targeting NVIDIA GPUs (with ongoing AMD support).

misconceptions.claim: Triton's IR is at the same level of abstraction as PyTorch tensor operations; there is no notion of block/tile.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Triton sits below tensor libraries: users choose block sizes, offsets and mask patterns explicitly, unlike PyTorch tensor ops.
